newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW - HK's TVB banks on handover happiness.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - HK's TVB banks on handover happiness.

text.p: Hong Kong's Television Broadcasts Ltd (TVB) expects local people to feel confident after the handover, spending more money and boosting the company's bottom line.

"After all the celebration, people are going to go back to work and some people will find that the changeover will be better for them," Alex Ying, TVB's general manager, corporate affairs, told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday.
Consumer spending has been sluggish over the last two years amid uncertainty over Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule.
"It's not like people do not have the money, it's just that they've been a little cautious over the last two years. But I think that spending will come back," he said.
The smoothness of the transition and expectations that strong growth in China will help Hong Kong down the road are driving the good feeling, said Ying.
As consumers spend more, companies advertise more, and that's good news for TVB.
So far this year, TVB has experienced a slight improvement in advertising revenues. "Revenues are better than last year, but there has been no dramatic turnaround," said Ying.

He said TVB's ratings have increased significantly this year, which bodes well for advertiser interest as the year progresses. TVB curently captures some 78-80 percent of Hong Kong's television advertising revenues.
Ying said the company expected positive profit growth this year after a decline in 1996.
"If everything is on course, then I think we should have profit growth this year," Ying said, adding "we should be in the low teens I think, at least."

The broadcasting and production company reported profit attributable to shareholders for the year ended December 31, 1996, of HK$477.2 million (US$61.2 million), a drop of 1.72 percent compared with 1995's HK$485.55 million.
TVB provides extensive programming in English and Cantonese in Hong Kong. It claims to be the world's largest producer of Chinese-language programming.
Demand for programming in Mandarin, the version of Chinese spoken in Beijing, is expected to rise once Hong Kong returns to the mainland.
But Ying said he did not expect an increase in Mandarin programming to come at the expense of English-language shows.
"I would say that both English language programming and Mandarin programming will increase," as consumers demand more choice, he said.
Increasingly, language is "no longer an issue" because technology now allows viewers to choose in which language they would like to receive programming, he said.
Ying said that despite widespread concerns that China might clamp down on Hong Kong's press freedoms, TVB has never been pressured by anyone to alter its programming.
"People talk about self-censorship, but if you censor your news what you are saying is that you are willing to forego that line of profit," said Ying.
"In the information market, if you don't report something and someone else does, then you are putting yourself in a competitive disadvantage that eventually works to your detriment," he said.
